extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in politics, media and broadcasting
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance (implicit) about using comedians as guests on serious political television programmes — when it's appropriate, the risks, and how it affects tone, messaging and perceived bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of inviting a comedian to a serious politics show
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether inviting a comedian onto a serious political programme is a suitable editorial choice, especially around high-profile interviews (e.g., an interview 'meant to be the highlight' of the debut episode).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics argued it was 'not the best idea' to invite Joe Lycett on a serious politics show; producers should weigh the show's goals and the importance of the interviewee when booking guests, particularly during high-stakes moments such as leadership contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of role and behaviour for comedian guests
rubrics_metrics.description: How clearly the comedian's role (entertainer vs analyst) is signalled and whether their expected behaviour (doing comedy) aligns with the programme's format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As Martin Lewis put it: 'You invite a comedian on a programme, expect them to do comedy.' Producers should set expectations for audience and viewers about whether a guest is there to provide analysis or to perform comedic commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and context sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the timing of comedic interventions is appropriate given the political context (e.g., 'on the eve of her expected election', national crises, or when the country faces serious problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some commenters said 'at a time when the country is facing a national crisis' a comic might be inappropriate; editorial teams should consider current events and public sentiment before allowing humour to interrupt serious interviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone management — avoiding lowering the programme's tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether comedic behaviour 'lowers the tone' of a programme into sarcastic, wise‑guy jabber rather than contributing constructively to discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Daily Mail accused Lycett of 'generally lowering the tone to the kind of sarcastic wise-guy jabber'; producers and guests should avoid antics that reduce credibility or the perceived seriousness of the show when serious discussion is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of humour as political critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether humour successfully challenges or exposes political actors and situations — e.g., 'when politics descends into farce, challenging it with humour is ... necessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour can be 'appropriate, but necessary' to call out political absurdity; consider whether the comedic approach illuminates or simply mocks without substantive critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of perceived broadcaster bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether comedic mockery of a political figure will be interpreted as partisan bias by audiences or media (e.g., accusations of 'anti-Tory bias').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BBC faced accusations of bias after Lycett's mockery; editorial teams must weigh the likelihood of bias claims and the impact on public trust when featuring partisan-targeting humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of overshadowing the interviewee and journalistic content
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a comedian's antics 'suck up all the attention' and overshadow the intended interview or the interviewee's messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics said Lycett 'sucked up all the attention' and 'overshadowed' the interview; consider guest placement and moderation to ensure the journalistic purpose of an interview isn't undermined by entertainment elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputational and political backlash management
rubrics_metrics.description: The potential for tabloid furore, political complaints, or calls for apology following comedic interventions on public-service broadcasts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Daily Mail reported calls for an apology and Tory figures criticised the segment; broadcasters should anticipate and manage reputational risks and be prepared for political fallout when commissioning or airing contentious comedic content.
